episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, May eleventh, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

M.I.T. faculty now update their A.I. course materials every six months and introduce entirely new courses as paradigms emerge within months rather than years. Deputy Dean of Academics Asuman Ozdaglar told Marketplace that a professor could once develop a class and teach it for twenty years with only minor yearly adjustments. That approach no longer works for A.I. courses, Ozdaglar said. M.I.T. designed its A.I.-D major before ChatGPT launched, anticipating demand for students who understand how to design, build, and deploy A.I. systems across the economy. The Electrical Engineering and Computer Science department created the program to teach students the full lifecycle of A.I. development, from initial design through real-world deployment. The major emphasizes foundational skills that will remain relevant as specific tools change, preparing graduates to adapt rather than master technologies that may become obsolete within a single academic year. M.I.T. built a human-centered component into the major to address ethical considerations alongside technical training.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to an update on a story we covered last week. Instructure, the company behind the Canvas learning management platform, has now paid attackers who breached the system during finals week. The breach exposed approximately two hundred seventy-five million records across more than eight thousand eight hundred institutions, according to Community College Daily. Canvas serves forty-one percent of U.S. higher education institutions. Jake Braun, head of the University of Chicago's Cyber Policy Initiative, told A.B.C. Seven Chicago that artificial intelligence was used in the attack. Braun said ransomware represents one of the fastest growing criminal enterprises in the world. Instructure claims to have received digital confirmation of data destruction, but Braun said the stolen personal information may still be circulating. Community colleges face disproportionate impact from the breach, with smaller I.T. staffs enduring longer downtime.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Meanwhile at M.I.T., a writing instructor recognized A.I.-generated prose in student assignments before the students admitted using the tools. Lecturer Micah Nathan, a novelist whose books include Gods of Aberdeen and Losing Graceland, wrote about the experience in The Guardian. Nathan described the A.I. output as polished but mediocre. Nathan wrote that students who delegate writing to A.I. skip the cognitive work that transforms unclear thoughts into structured arguments. The printing press and telephone sparked similar debates in the past, Nathan noted, but A.I. differs because it handles the thinking process itself rather than simply speeding up communication.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In research news, Stanford researchers are using large language models to analyze text archives at scales that were previously impossible. Sociologist Amir Goldberg analyzed fourteen point seven million workplace emails to measure the overlap between employees' self-identity and their collective workplace identity. Goldberg also analyzed four point two million court decisions in separate studies. Other Stanford faculty have assembled more than seven hundred eighty thousand corporate earnings call transcripts from more than twenty-one thousand companies, running the text through large language models on Stanford's computing clusters. Goldberg told Stanford Report that large language models give researchers an instrument that allows them to examine historical patterns across massive text archives.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told Carnegie Mellon University graduates that A.I. is not likely to replace them, but that someone skilled in A.I. could replace someone without those capabilities. Huang delivered the commencement address in Pittsburgh and compared the current moment to the dawn of the personal computer revolution. Huang said graduates are entering the job market at an extraordinary moment. A new era of science and discovery is beginning, Huang said, and A.I. will accelerate the expansion of human knowledge and help solve problems once beyond reach. Huang explicitly countered warnings from other tech leaders who have predicted A.I. could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And at Cal Poly Pomona, students now have access to four high-performance G.P.U. servers through a new A.I. Sandbox that opens industry-level computing to undergraduates across all disciplines. The servers, donated by the nonprofit Computing for Humanity, provide shared on-campus computing without commercial cloud platform costs. Unlike typical university research setups that require faculty sponsorship, the A.I. Sandbox is open to any student. Marketing students use it for sentiment analysis. Environmental studies students access scientific datasets and modeling tools. Students build and manage systems through hands-on tasks including hardware installation and software configuration.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: MIT Updates A.I. Curriculum Every Six Months as Field Outpaces Traditional Course Design
leadStory.summary: MIT faculty update their A.I. course materials every six months and introduce entirely new courses as paradigms emerge within months rather than years, Deputy Dean of Academics Asuman Ozdaglar told Marketplace in an interview about the university's approach to A.I. education. Ozdaglar said a professor could once develop a class and teach it for twenty years with only minor yearly adjustments. That approach no longer works for A.I. courses, Ozdaglar said. MIT designed its AI-D major before ChatGPT launched, anticipating demand for students who understand how to design, build, and deploy A.I. systems across the economy. The Electrical Engineering and Computer Science department created the program to teach students the full lifecycle of A.I. development, from initial design through real-world deployment across multiple industries and business sectors. Students learn to build A.I. systems, understand how they work internally, and deploy them responsibly in various applications. The major emphasizes foundational skills that will remain relevant as specific tools change, preparing graduates to adapt rather than master technologies that may become obsolete within a single academic year. Ozdaglar noted that A.I.'s accessibility through natural language interfaces means anyone can now interact with A.I. systems without any technical training whatsoever. MIT built a human-centered component into the major to address ethical considerations alongside technical training. The curriculum positions ethical reasoning as critical to the technology's development rather than as an optional addition. Before A.I., course content at universities often remained stable for decades without major updates, Ozdaglar said. The six-month update cycle now required for A.I. courses reflects the pace of change in the field.

quickHits.headline: Instructure Paid Ransom After Canvas Breach Exposed 275 Million Records
quickHits.summary: Instructure, the company behind Canvas, paid attackers who breached the learning management platform during finals week, an update on a story first reported here on May 7. The breach exposed approximately 275 million records across 8,809 institutions, according to Community College Daily. Canvas serves 41 percent of U.S. higher education institutions. Jake Braun, head of the University of Chicago's Cyber Policy Initiative and former White House deputy national cyber director, told ABC7 Chicago that artificial intelligence was used in the attack. Braun said ransomware represents one of the fastest growing criminal enterprises in the world. Instructure claims to have received digital confirmation of data destruction, but Braun said the stolen personal information may still be circulating. The hackers exploited Free-For-Teacher accounts and compromised Instructure twice within nine days. Community colleges face disproportionate impact from the breach, with smaller IT staffs enduring longer downtime and tighter budgets forcing difficult choices between security subscriptions and instructional funding.

quickHits.headline: MIT Writing Instructor Identifies A.I.-Generated Student Work Before Students Admit Using It
quickHits.summary: A.I.-generated student writing is detectable but lacks the developmental value of human effort, MIT lecturer Micah Nathan wrote in an essay for The Guardian. Nathan, a novelist whose books include Gods of Aberdeen and Losing Graceland, teaches fiction and nonfiction writing classes at the university. Nathan wrote that he identified A.I.-generated prose in student assignments before the students admitted using the tools. Nathan described the A.I. output as "polished but mediocre" in the essay. Nathan wrote that students who delegate writing to A.I. skip the cognitive work that transforms unclear thoughts into more structured arguments. The printing press and telephone sparked similar debates in the past, Nathan noted. But A.I. differs from those earlier technologies, Nathan wrote, because it handles the thinking process itself rather than simply speeding up communication. Nathan's essay focused on his direct observations from teaching fiction and nonfiction writing courses at MIT over recent academic semesters.

quickHits.headline: Stanford Researchers Use A.I. to Analyze Millions of Emails, Court Decisions, and Corporate Documents
quickHits.summary: Stanford researchers are using large language models to analyze text archives at scales that were previously impossible for academic research. Sociologist Amir Goldberg, co-director of the university's Computational Culture Lab, analyzed 14.7 million workplace emails to measure the overlap between employees' self-identity and their collective workplace identity. Goldberg also analyzed 4.2 million court decisions in separate studies examining how ideas move from the margins into the mainstream over time. Goldberg told Stanford Report that large language models give researchers an instrument that allows them to examine historical patterns across massive text archives. Other Stanford faculty have assembled more than 780,000 corporate earnings call transcripts from more than 21,000 companies, running the text through large language models on Stanford's computing clusters to identify patterns across decades of corporate communications. Goldberg described the digital traces of modern life as an informational treasure trove for researchers. The work demonstrates how A.I. tools are enabling analysis at scales that reshape entire academic fields.

quickHits.headline: Nvidia CEO Tells Carnegie Mellon Graduates A.I. Will Not Replace Them
quickHits.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told Carnegie Mellon University graduates that A.I. is not likely to replace them, but that someone skilled in A.I. could replace someone without those capabilities. Huang delivered the commencement address in Pittsburgh on May eleventh and compared the current moment to the dawn of the personal computer revolution. Huang said graduates are entering the job market at an extraordinary moment in the technology industry. Huang said a new era of science and discovery is beginning and that A.I. will accelerate the expansion of human knowledge and help solve problems once beyond reach. Huang, who graduated from Oregon State University in 1984 and cofounded Nvidia in 1993, explicitly countered warnings from tech leaders including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has predicted A.I. could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs. Huang said that when society engages technology openly, responsibly, and optimistically, it expands human potential far more than it diminishes it.

quickHits.headline: Cal Poly Pomona Opens A.I. Sandbox With Industry-Grade Computing for All Students
quickHits.summary: Cal Poly Pomona students now have access to four high-performance Supermicro GPU servers through a new A.I. Sandbox that opens industry-level computing to undergraduates across all disciplines. The servers, donated by the nonprofit Computing for Humanity, provide shared on-campus computing without commercial cloud platform costs. Unlike typical university research setups that require faculty sponsorship, the A.I. Sandbox is open to any student. Marketing students use it for sentiment analysis across surveys and social media. Environmental studies students access scientific datasets and modeling tools. Information security students gain infrastructure management experience. Roy Chartier, founder of Computing for Humanity, said the partnership expands equitable access to high-performance computing and helps enable the next generation of researchers, builders, and innovators. Students build and manage systems through hands-on tasks including hardware installation and software configuration. Bill Luong, a graduate student and system administrator on the project, said the team designed the A.I. Sandbox with a student-first perspective.
